# Roadside Tube Patch Guide

You need: tire levers (2 or 3), a patch kit (patches, rubber cement or self-adhesive, sandpaper or a scuffer), a pump or CO2 inflator, and a tube that has the hole. Work on a flat, dry spot if you can.

## Part 1: Find the flat

1. Check the tire for the object that caused the flat. Run your fingers slowly around the inside and outside of the tire. Remove any glass, thorn, or wire you find. If you skip this, the new patch will fail fast.
2. Note where the object went through. Mark the spot on the tire with a pen if you have one.

## Part 2: Remove the wheel

3. Shift the bike into the smallest rear cog (or the gear that makes the wheel easiest to remove). This takes tension off the chain.
4. Open the brake quick release if the bike has one. For rim brakes, the lever or quick release opens the caliper so the tire clears the brake pads. For disc brakes, do not squeeze the brake lever while the wheel is out.
5. Front wheel: open the quick release lever (or undo the nuts or axle bolts). Lift the wheel out of the fork.
6. Rear wheel: lift the chain off the smallest cog if needed, then pull the wheel out of the frame. Hold the derailleur out of the way.

## Part 3: Remove the tire

7. Deflate the tube completely. Press the valve core (the pin in the valve tip) with a fingernail or small tool to let air out. For a Presta valve, unscrew the top nut first, then press the pin.
8. Push the bead (the tire edge) off the rim on both sides, all the way around, so the tire pulls free on one side.
9. Hook a tire lever under the bead at one spot, about 10 cm from the valve. Pull the lever toward the spokes so the bead comes over the rim edge. Hook a second lever a few spots away and pull it along the rim to pop the bead off.
10. Use a third lever only if needed. Do not use screwdrivers, they can pinch and cut the tube.
11. Once one side of the tire is off, pull the tube out through the gap. Keep the tire on the bike if you can, so you can check the inside for the sharp object.

## Part 4: Find and mark the hole

12. Pump the tube with a little air, just enough to round it out.
13. Find the leak. Listen for a hiss, or run your wet fingers or spit along the tube. Bubbles mark the hole.
14. Mark the hole with a pen or the chalk from the kit. Let the tube go flat again.

## Part 5: Patch the tube

15. Dry and clean the area around the hole. Rub it with sandpaper or the scuffer from the kit for about 2 cm around the hole. This roughens the rubber so the glue grips.
16. Apply a thin layer of rubber cement to the scuffed area. Let it dry until it looks dull or tacky, usually 1 to 3 minutes. Do not touch it with your fingers.
17. If you use self-adhesive patches: peel the backing and press the patch firmly over the hole. If you use cement patches: spread a thin coat on the patch, let it dry, then press it on.
18. Press firmly for about 30 seconds. Make sure the edges are sealed all the way around.
19. Wait the time the kit label gives (often 2 to 5 minutes). Do not inflate early.

## Part 6: Check for the cause

20. Before the tube goes back, look again at the tire where the object went through. Feel inside and outside. Remove the object if it is still there.
21. If the object is still in the tire, the new tube will also go flat. Tape or a boot is a helpful fix for small cuts in the tire. A boot can be a piece of folded cardboard, a dollar bill, or a patch from the kit placed inside the tire.

## Part 7: Put the tube back

22. Put a small amount of air in the tube, just enough to give it shape. This stops it from folding and getting pinched.
23. Insert the valve into the valve hole on the rim first. Tuck the rest of the tube inside the tire, all the way around, so no part is caught between the tire and the rim.
24. Push the tire bead back onto the rim, starting opposite the valve and working toward it. Use your thumbs. The last section near the valve is the hardest. Use a lever carefully if needed, but watch the tube.
25. Check that the tube is not pinched at the bead on either side. Pinch flats happen here.

## Part 8: Inflate and reinstall

26. Inflate slowly. Check the tire is seated evenly on the rim. There should be an even line around the tire edge.
27. Inflate to the pressure printed on the tire sidewall (the range is often 65 to 100 PSI for road tires, check your tire). Do not exceed the maximum on the sidewall.
28. Put the wheel back in the frame. Front: seat the axle in the fork dropouts, then close the quick release firmly. Rear: lay the chain on the smallest cog, then seat the axle in the dropouts.
29. Reconnect the brake. Spin the wheel to check it clears the frame and brake pads.
30. Test the brakes. Squeeze each lever and make sure the wheel stops.

## Part 9: Final check

31. Spin the wheel by hand and watch for wobble or rubbing.
32. Squeeze the tire to check firmness. Ride a short distance slowly before going fast.

## Tips

- Carry a spare tube. Patching works, but a spare gets you rolling faster.
- Patch kits can fail when the glue is still wet or the surface is dusty. Let the glue dry fully.
- If the patch leaks again, the cement may not have been dry, or the hole may be too close to the valve or the tube seam.
- If a tube has more than two or three holes, replace it.

# Chain and Cassette Wear

## Why chains wear out

A bicycle chain is a row of small steel plates joined by pins and rollers. Each link moves against the next one thousands of times per ride. Grit from the road gets between the pins and the inner plates and grinds them down. The pin wears a little, the hole it sits in gets slightly larger, and every link becomes a bit longer than it was when new. This stretch is called elongation. The chain does not actually stretch like rubber. The metal wears so the distance between pins grows.

Dirt and dry lubricant speed this up. Riding in rain, mud, or sand, and skipping cleaning or lubrication, makes wear much faster. Heavy riders, hard pedaling, and frequent shifting under load also add wear.

## How long the chain lasts

With normal care, a chain often lasts 2,000 to 4,000 miles (about 3,000 to 6,500 km). Wet or gritty riding can cut that roughly in half. Stop judging by mileage alone and measure the chain.

## How to measure wear

The standard pitch on modern bicycle chains is 1/2 inch (12.7 mm). That means 24 links, pin center to pin center, span exactly 12 inches on a new chain.

**Method 1: Chain checker tool (most accurate, about 10 to 20 dollars)**
1. Clean the chain so grit does not affect the reading.
2. Hook the tool's small pin into a chain link and let the tool sit flat.
3. Read the indicator. Most checkers show a reading for 0.5 percent and 0.75 percent wear.
4. Check the chain in several spots, because a chain does not wear evenly.

**Method 2: Ruler (works with no tool)**
1. Clean the chain and shift to the largest rear cog and the middle front ring, so the chain is not under stress.
2. Use a ruler or tape measure. Measure from the center of one pin to the center of the pin 12 inches further along. Count 24 links to find the exact point.
3. A new chain reads 12.00 inches.
4. At 0.5 percent wear, the reading is about 12.06 inches. At 0.75 percent wear, the reading is about 12.09 inches.
5. Measure in more than one place along the chain.

## When to replace the chain

- **Replace at 0.5 to 0.75 percent wear.** Most mechanics replace the chain at this point. The cassette and chainrings are still in good shape, so a new chain costs much less than new cassette and rings.
- **Above 0.75 percent, replace the chain right away.** Past this point, the chain starts to damage the cassette and chainrings.
- **Signs without a tool:** the chain skips under load, makes grinding or clicking noises, has stiff or rusty links, or shifts poorly.

## Cassette and chainring wear

The cassette is the set of rear cogs. Worn cogs look and feel like this:

- The teeth look hooked or shark-fin shaped, with the back edge sharpened into a point.
- Teeth are thin, pointed, or have uneven tops.
- The chain skips or slips under pedal force, especially on the largest or most-used cogs.
- The chain sits too far down into the cog teeth.

A worn chain wears the cassette because the stretched pins do not sit correctly in the cog teeth. Once a cassette has worn into this shape, a new chain will skip on it. That means the cassette must be replaced as well.

## When to replace the cassette

Replace the cassette when:

- The teeth are hooked or pointed (shark-fin shape), or
- A new chain skips under load on it, or
- A chain measures above 0.75 percent and the cassette is worn.

In most cases, replacing the chain before 0.75 percent wear saves the cassette. A typical cassette lasts two to three chains if you change the chain on time. Chain and cassette should be replaced as a matched set when the cassette is worn, and you should check that the new chain matches the number of speeds on the cassette (for example, 10 speed, 11 speed, or 12 speed).

## Quick summary

1. Measure the chain every few hundred miles with a checker or a ruler.
2. Replace the chain at 0.5 to 0.75 percent wear.
3. Check the cassette and chainrings every time you replace the chain.
4. Replace the cassette when the teeth are hooked, or when a new chain skips on it.

# Week-Long Bike Tour Packing Guide

Assumptions: self-supported touring, about 50 to 90 km per day, mixed weather, one bike, panniers or a rack bag setup, and one carry-on plus one checked bag if you fly with the bike. Adjust quantities if your route, climate, or lodging differs.

## 1. Bike and flight prep
- Bike box or soft case: protects the frame and drivetrain in transit. Airlines often damage unprotected bikes.
- Remove pedals, turn handlebars parallel to the frame, deflate tires to about 30 percent of working pressure, and wrap the derailleur. Less stress on the frame and derailleur hanger, and the box fits.
- Pack a spare derailleur hanger, a few spare bolts, and a chain tool. Hangers bend in transit, and a spare lets you keep riding.
- Keep tires, tubes, and pedals with you in the carry-on if the airline allows. Tools in the checked bag can be taken out at check-in.

## 2. Repair kit (carry on the bike at all times)
- Two spare inner tubes, matched to your tire size. Punctures are the most common tour failure.
- Tire levers (three). Old tires need them, and one snaps.
- Compact pump or CO2 inflator with two cartridges. A pump is reusable; CO2 is fast but runs out.
- Multitool with hex keys, Torx, and a chain breaker. Covers most roadside adjustments.
- Quick link or spare chain pin for your chain type. A broken chain otherwise ends the day.
- Patch kit and a spare tire boot (a folded piece of tough plastic or a dollar bill works in a pinch).
- Spoke wrench and a spare spoke if your wheels are hand built or your route is remote.
- Small bottle of chain lube and rags. Dry chains wear faster and get noisy.
- Brake pads: one spare pair, since long descents wear pads quickly.

## 3. Clothing (plan for 4 to 5 days, do laundry on the way)
- Cycling shorts with padding: two pairs. Padding is the single biggest comfort factor on long days. Rotate to let one pair dry.
- Cycling jerseys: three. Wicking fabric dries overnight.
- Base layer, long sleeve: one. Warm mornings and cold descents.
- Warm layer: one lightweight insulated jacket or fleece. Cold rain and high passes lower temperatures quickly.
- Waterproof shell: one rain jacket. Rain jacket and rain pants if rain is likely.
- Cycling gloves: one pair. Protects palms in a fall and cushions the bars.
- Arm warmers or leg warmers: one each, optional. Cover cold mornings and cool down.
- Casual clothes for evenings: one pair of pants or shorts, one shirt. You want something other than cycling clothes at dinner.
- Underwear and socks: six pairs of socks, six underwear. Change daily; socks cause blisters when damp.
- Sleepwear: one set, light.
- Sun hat or cap with brim, and a buff or neck gaiter. Sun and wind protection.
- Cycling shoes or sturdy walking shoes: one pair worn on the plane. Carry flip flops or sandals for showers and evenings.

## 4. Helmet, eyewear, and visibility
- Helmet: worn on the plane or in the box. Required on many tours and it protects you on day one.
- Sunglasses with a spare lens or case. Protect from sun, wind, and insects.
- Front light and rear light with spare batteries or a USB charger. Required after dark and useful in tunnels.
- Reflective vest or bands. Visibility on busy roads.

## 5. Sleep and camp or lodging gear
- If you use hotels or hostels: a small sleep sheet or travel towel and earplugs. Reduces cost of bedding and loud rooms.
- If you camp: tent, sleeping bag rated for the lowest night temperature, sleeping pad, and a headlamp. These add weight, so consider lodging on the route.
- Headlamp: useful even with lodging, for dark bathrooms and early departures.

## 6. Toiletries and health
- Travel-size shampoo, soap, toothbrush, toothpaste, deodorant. Bike touring means limited laundry and showers.
- Sunscreen SPF 30 or higher, lip balm with SPF. Long days in sun cause burns.
- Chamois cream: reduces saddle sores and chafing on long days.
- Anti-chafe balm for thighs and underarms. Chafing ruins days faster than soreness.
- Blister plasters and a small first aid kit: antiseptic, bandages, pain relievers, anti-diarrhea tablets, rehydration salts, and any personal prescriptions in original containers.
- Insect repellent. Mosquitoes and ticks are common on rural routes.
- Hand sanitizer and a small towel.

## 7. Electronics and documents
- Phone with offline maps downloaded for the entire route. Cell coverage is patchy on rural roads.
- Cycling computer or GPS with a charged battery, plus its mount.
- Cables and a power bank of at least 10,000 mAh. Charge the bank before each day's ride.
- Plug adapter for the destination.
- Passport or ID, travel insurance card, and emergency contact list on paper.
- Cash in local currency and one backup card. Rural areas may not accept cards.

## 8. Bags and organization
- Two pannier bags or one rack bag and a handlebar bag. Keeps weight low and balanced.
- Waterproof stuff sacks or dry bags inside panniers. Rain soaks unprotected gear quickly.
- Small zip bags for toiletries, electronics, and documents. Keeps spills from reaching clothes.
- Hydration bottles or a bladder, plus two cages. Heat and climbs drain water fast.

## 9. Food and water
- Lightweight stove and fuel only if you plan to cook. Check airline rules for fuel.
- Electrolyte tablets or powder. Replaces salt lost while sweating.
- Energy bars and snacks: two to three per day, kept accessible in a jersey pocket. Low energy on climbs is a common failure.
- Water filter or purification tablets for remote areas.

## 10. Final checks before departure
- Confirm the airline's bike fee and size limits. Each airline sets its own limits.
- Confirm lodging bookings and check whether the bike can be stored safely there.
- Test-ride the loaded bike for 20 minutes to confirm the balance and braking.
- Remove or cover sharp edges on the bike box and label it with your name and contact information.
- Keep the repair kit, documents, and medications in the carry-on, not the checked bag.

## Weight tip
Aim for a total load under 10 percent of your body weight, not counting the bike. Heavier loads slow climbs and stress the rear wheel.

- Cycling gloves: one pair. Protects palms in a fall and cushions the bars.
- Arm warmers or leg warmers: one each, optional. Cover cold mornings and cool down.
- Casual clothes for evenings: one pair of pants or shorts, one shirt. You want something other than cycling clothes at dinner.
- Underwear and socks: six pairs of socks, six underwear. Change daily; socks cause blisters when damp.
- Sleepwear: one set, light.
- Sun hat or cap with brim, and a buff or neck gaiter. Sun and wind protection.
- Cycling shoes or sturdy walking shoes: one pair worn on the plane. Carry flip flops or sandals for showers and evenings.

## 4. Helmet, eyewear, and visibility
- Helmet: worn on the plane or in the box. Required on many tours and it protects you on day one.
- Sunglasses with a spare lens or case. Protect from sun, wind, and insects.
- Front light and rear light with spare batteries or a USB charger. Required after dark and useful in tunnels.
- Reflective vest or bands. Visibility on busy roads.

## 5. Sleep and camp or lodging gear
- If you use hotels or hostels: a small sleep sheet or travel towel and earplugs. Reduces cost of bedding and loud rooms.
- If you camp: tent, sleeping bag rated for the lowest night temperature, sleeping pad, and a headlamp. These add weight, so consider lodging on the route.
- Headlamp: useful even with lodging, for dark bathrooms and early departures.

## 6. Toiletries and health
- Travel-size shampoo, soap, toothbrush, toothpaste, deodorant. Bike touring means limited laundry and showers.
- Sunscreen SPF 30 or higher, lip balm with SPF. Long days in sun cause burns.
- Chamois cream: reduces saddle sores and chafing on long days.
- Anti-chafe balm for thighs and underarms. Chafing ruins days faster than soreness.
- Blister plasters and a small first aid kit: antiseptic, bandages, pain relievers, anti-diarrhea tablets, rehydration salts, and any personal prescriptions in original containers.
- Insect repellent. Mosquitoes and ticks are common on rural routes.
- Hand sanitizer and a small towel.

## 7. Electronics and documents
- Phone with offline maps downloaded for the entire route. Cell coverage is patchy on rural roads.
- Cycling computer or GPS with a charged battery, plus its mount.
- Cables and a power bank of at least 10,000 mAh. Charge the bank before each day's ride.
- Plug adapter for the destination.
- Passport or ID, travel insurance card, and emergency contact list on paper.
- Cash in local currency and one backup card. Rural areas may not accept cards.

## 8. Bags and organization
- Two pannier bags or one rack bag and a handlebar bag. Keeps weight low and balanced.
- Waterproof stuff sacks or dry bags inside panniers. Rain soaks unprotected gear quickly.
- Small zip bags for toiletries, electronics, and documents. Keeps spills from reaching clothes.
- Hydration bottles or a bladder, plus two cages. Heat and climbs drain water fast.

## 9. Food and water
- Lightweight stove and fuel only if you plan to cook. Check airline rules for fuel.
- Electrolyte tablets or powder. Replaces salt lost while sweating.
- Energy bars and snacks: two to three per day, kept accessible in a jersey pocket. Low energy on climbs is a common failure.
- Water filter or purification tablets for remote areas.

## 10. Final checks before departure
- Confirm the airline's bike fee and size limits. Each airline sets its own limits.
- Confirm lodging bookings and check whether the bike can be stored safely there.
- Test-ride the loaded bike for 20 minutes to confirm the balance and braking.
- Remove or cover sharp edges on the bike box and label it with your name and contact information.
- Keep the repair kit, documents, and medications in the carry-on, not the checked bag.

## Weight tip
Aim for a total load under 10 percent of your body weight, not counting the bike. Heavier loads slow climbs and stress the rear wheel.

# Roadside Tube Patch Guide

This guide walks you through fixing a flat tube with a patch kit, using only tools you carry on a ride. Read all the steps once before you start.

## What you need

- Tire levers (two or three, plastic or metal)
- Patch kit: sandpaper or metal scraper, rubber cement or glue, a few patches
- Small pump or CO2 inflator
- Spare tube (optional, but the fastest fix)
- A way to find the hole: a bowl of water, or your cheek and ears
- A rag or shop towel

## Step 1: Stop safely and get the wheel off

1. Pull over on flat ground, away from traffic. Put the bike on its stand or lean it against a fence or tree.
2. If the rear wheel is flat, shift the chain onto the smallest rear cog. This gives slack.
3. Open the brake quick release if your bike has one. For a rear wheel, lift the derailleur and pull the wheel out. For a front wheel, open the quick release and lift the wheel out.

## Step 2: Let out the rest of the air

1. Unscrew the valve cap.
2. Press the valve core pin briefly to make sure all air is gone. Presta valves (thin, with a small nut on top) need the nut unscrewed first, then press the pin.
3. Squeeze the tire to confirm it is fully flat.

## Step 3: Break the bead

The bead is the edge of the tire that sits in the rim. You must push it off the rim to reach the tube.

1. Push both sides of the tire toward the center of the rim all the way around. This loosens the bead.
2. Work on the side opposite the valve first. Push the tire edge into the center well of the rim.

## Step 4: Remove the tube

1. Push one tire lever under the bead, about 10 cm from the valve. Hook the lever over a spoke. Do not pinch the tube.
2. Pull the lever toward the spoke. Pry the bead up and over the rim edge.
3. Use a second lever a hand width away from the first. Hook it under the bead and pry it over the rim. Keep the first lever in place.
4. Use a third lever only if the bead is stubborn.
5. Remove the lever closest to the valve. Unhook the valve from the rim hole and pull the tube out of the tire, starting at the valve.

## Step 5: Find the hole

1. Pump a little air into the tube so it is slightly round.
2. Listen for a hiss. Run your cheek or the back of your fingers along the tube slowly.
3. If you cannot find it, dunk sections of the tube in water and look for bubbles.
4. Mark the hole with a pen or by pressing a bit of dirt into it.
5. Check the inside of the tire for the cause. Run your fingers slowly around the inside of the tire. Remove any glass, thorn, or wire. A tire with a cut must be fixed before you reinstall the tube, or the new hole will come back quickly.

## Step 6: Prepare the patch area

1. Dry the area around the hole with a rag.
2. Use the sandpaper or scraper to rough up a patch-sized area around the hole. Roughen about 2 cm across. Do not sand through the rubber.
3. Wipe away the dust with a clean part of the rag.

## Step 7: Apply the glue

1. Squeeze a small amount of rubber cement onto the roughened area. Spread it in a thin layer about the size of the patch.
2. Wait until the glue is tacky. Touch it with a fingertip. It should feel sticky but not wet. This usually takes one to three minutes.

## Step 8: Apply the patch

1. Peel the foil backing off the patch. Do not touch the sticky side with your fingers.
2. Center the patch over the hole.
3. Press the patch down firmly for 30 seconds. Work from the center outward to push out air bubbles.
4. Leave the foil on the patch if the kit says to. Some kits need the foil removed after a short wait.

## Step 9: Check the tube before reinstalling

1. Lightly dust the patch with talc or sand if the kit includes it. This stops the tube from sticking to the tire.
2. Pump a little air in and test the patch in the water bowl if you have one. No bubbles should come out.

## Step 10: Put the tube back in the tire

1. Pump the tube slightly, just enough to give it shape.
2. Insert the valve into the rim hole first. Then tuck the tube into the tire all the way around.
3. Keep the tube inside the tire, not caught between the tire and the rim. A pinched tube will fail quickly.
4. Check the tube sits evenly all the way around.

## Step 11: Seat the tire on the rim

1. Push the tire bead back onto the rim, starting at the valve and working in both directions.
2. Use your hands first. Push the bead toward the center well of the rim, then use the last section to bring it up over the edge.
3. If the last section is tight, use a tire lever carefully. Do not pinch the tube.
4. Check that the tube is not showing between the tire and rim at any point.

## Step 12: Inflate

1. Pump a little air in to round the tube. Check the bead on both sides for even seating.
2. Pump to the pressure printed on the tire sidewall. Use a gauge if you have one. Hand pumping is fine for a roadside repair.
3. Spin the wheel and check for wobble or rubbing on the brake pad.

## Step 13: Reinstall the wheel

1. Put the wheel back in the frame. Make sure the axle sits fully in the dropouts.
2. Close the quick release or tighten the axle nuts. For a rear wheel, make sure the chain sits on the smallest cog while you thread the wheel in, then shift back to a comfortable gear.
3. Check the brake pads are not rubbing the tire.
4. Spin the wheel. It should turn freely.

## After the repair

- Ride gently for the first few minutes and watch for soft tire pressure.
- Patches are a temporary fix. Replace the tube at the next shop visit, or sooner if the patch area is damaged or the tube was pinched.
- If the tube leaks again after a patch, check the tire for debris before you try a second patch.

## Quick troubleshooting

- Tube goes flat again soon: The patch did not seal, or the tire still has a sharp object inside. Check both.
- Patch peels off: The area was not roughened enough, or the glue was not tacky. Clean and try again.
- Tire will not seat on rim: Check for a pinched tube or the wrong tire size. Make sure the tire is not twisted.
- Valve leaks: Tighten the valve core or the lock nut. Replace the tube if it still leaks.

5. Remove the lever closest to the valve. Unhook the valve from the rim hole and pull the tube out of the tire, starting at the valve.

## Step 5: Find the hole

1. Pump a little air into the tube so it is slightly round.
2. Listen for a hiss. Run your cheek or the back of your fingers along the tube slowly.
3. If you cannot find it, dunk sections of the tube in water and look for bubbles.
4. Mark the hole with a pen or by pressing a bit of dirt into it.
5. Check the inside of the tire for the cause. Run your fingers slowly around the inside of the tire. Remove any glass, thorn, or wire. A tire with a cut must be fixed before you reinstall the tube, or the new hole will come back quickly.

## Step 6: Prepare the patch area

1. Dry the area around the hole with a rag.
2. Use the sandpaper or scraper to rough up a patch-sized area around the hole. Roughen about 2 cm across. Do not sand through the rubber.
3. Wipe away the dust with a clean part of the rag.

## Step 7: Apply the glue

1. Squeeze a small amount of rubber cement onto the roughened area. Spread it in a thin layer about the size of the patch.
2. Wait until the glue is tacky. Touch it with a fingertip. It should feel sticky but not wet. This usually takes one to three minutes.

## Step 8: Apply the patch

1. Peel the foil backing off the patch. Do not touch the sticky side with your fingers.
2. Center the patch over the hole.
3. Press the patch down firmly for 30 seconds. Work from the center outward to push out air bubbles.
4. Leave the foil on the patch if the kit says to. Some kits need the foil removed after a short wait.

## Step 9: Check the tube before reinstalling

1. Lightly dust the patch with talc or sand if the kit includes it. This stops the tube from sticking to the tire.
2. Pump a little air in and test the patch in the water bowl if you have one. No bubbles should come out.

## Step 10: Put the tube back in the tire

1. Pump the tube slightly, just enough to give it shape.
2. Insert the valve into the rim hole first. Then tuck the tube into the tire all the way around.
3. Keep the tube inside the tire, not caught between the tire and the rim. A pinched tube will fail quickly.
4. Check the tube sits evenly all the way around.

## Step 11: Seat the tire on the rim

1. Push the tire bead back onto the rim, starting at the valve and working in both directions.
2. Use your hands first. Push the bead toward the center well of the rim, then use the last section to bring it up over the edge.
3. If the last section is tight, use a tire lever carefully. Do not pinch the tube.
4. Check that the tube is not showing between the tire and rim at any point.

## Step 12: Inflate

1. Pump a little air in to round the tube. Check the bead on both sides for even seating.
2. Pump to the pressure printed on the tire sidewall. Use a gauge if you have one. Hand pumping is fine for a roadside repair.
3. Spin the wheel and check for wobble or rubbing on the brake pad.

## Step 13: Reinstall the wheel

1. Put the wheel back in the frame. Make sure the axle sits fully in the dropouts.
2. Close the quick release or tighten the axle nuts. For a rear wheel, make sure the chain sits on the smallest cog while you thread the wheel in, then shift back to a comfortable gear.
3. Check the brake pads are not rubbing the tire.
4. Spin the wheel. It should turn freely.

## After the repair

- Ride gently for the first few minutes and watch for soft tire pressure.
- Patches are a temporary fix. Replace the tube at the next shop visit, or sooner if the patch area is damaged or the tube was pinched.
- If the tube leaks again after a patch, check the tire for debris before you try a second patch.

## Quick troubleshooting

- Tube goes flat again soon: The patch did not seal, or the tire still has a sharp object inside. Check both.
- Patch peels off: The area was not roughened enough, or the glue was not tacky. Clean and try again.
- Tire will not seat on rim: Check for a pinched tube or the wrong tire size. Make sure the tire is not twisted.
- Valve leaks: Tighten the valve core or the lock nut. Replace the tube if it still leaks.

This guide walks you through fixing a flat tube with a patch kit, using only tools you carry on a ride. Read all the steps once before you start.

## What you need

- Tire levers (two or three, plastic or metal)
- Patch kit: sandpaper or metal scraper, rubber cement or glue, a few patches
- Small pump or CO2 inflator
- Spare tube (optional, but the fastest fix)
- A way to find the hole: a bowl of water, or your cheek and ears
- A rag or shop towel

## Step 1: Stop safely and get the wheel off

1. Pull over on flat ground, away from traffic. Put the bike on its stand or lean it against a fence or tree.
2. If the rear wheel is flat, shift the chain onto the smallest rear cog. This gives slack.
3. Open the brake quick release if your bike has one. For a rear wheel, lift the derailleur and pull the wheel out. For a front wheel, open the quick release and lift the wheel out.

## Step 2: Let out the rest of the air

1. Unscrew the valve cap.
2. Press the valve core pin briefly to make sure all air is gone. Presta valves (thin, with a small nut on top) need the nut unscrewed first, then press the pin.
3. Squeeze the tire to confirm it is fully flat.

## Step 3: Break the bead

The bead is the edge of the tire that sits in the rim. You must push it off the rim to reach the tube.

1. Push both sides of the tire toward the center of the rim all the way around. This loosens the bead.
2. Work on the side opposite the valve first. Push the tire edge into the center well of the rim.

## Step 4: Remove the tube

1. Push one tire lever under the bead, about 10 cm from the valve. Hook the lever over a spoke. Do not pinch the tube.
2. Pull the lever toward the spoke. Pry the bead up and over the rim edge.
3. Use a second lever a hand width away from the first. Hook it under the bead and pry it over the rim. Keep the first lever in place.
4. Use a third lever only if the bead is stubborn.

2. Center the patch over the hole.
3. Press the patch down firmly for 30 seconds. Work from the center outward to push out air bubbles.
4. Leave the foil on the patch if the kit says to. Some kits need the foil removed after a short wait.

## Step 9: Check the tube before reinstalling

1. Lightly dust the patch with talc or sand if the kit includes it. This stops the tube from sticking to the tire.

## Step 11: Seat the tire on the rim

1. Push the tire bead back onto the rim, starting at the valve and working in both directions.
2. Use your hands first. Push the bead toward the center well of the rim, then use the last section to bring it up over the edge.

# Patching a Bike Tube at the Roadside

Allow about 30 to 45 minutes the first time. Work slowly and keep small parts like valve caps and patches away from the road.

## What you need

1. Two or three tire levers (plastic is best, metal can pinch the tube).
2. A pump or CO2 inflator.
3. A patch kit with glue, patches, and sandpaper or a scuffer.
4. A spare tube, if you have one. A spare is often faster than patching.
5. A wrench for the axle nuts, if your wheel uses nuts instead of a quick release lever.
6. A piece of cloth or a folded dollar bill for a tire boot, if the tire itself is cut.

## Step 1: Prepare the bike

1. Stand the bike up or turn it upside down on its saddle and handlebars.
2. If the rear tire is flat, shift the chain to the smallest rear cog. This removes chain tension so the wheel comes out easily.
3. Open the brake. On rim brakes, use the quick release on the brake arms or the cable release. On disc brakes, leave the brake alone and just avoid touching the rotor.
4. Open the wheel quick release lever by flipping it outward, or loosen the axle nuts with a wrench.
5. Lift the wheel out. For the rear wheel, lift the chain off the cog and pull the wheel forward and down.

## Step 2: Let out the rest of the air

1. Look at the valve. A Schrader valve looks like a car tire valve. A Presta valve is thinner with a small lock nut on top.
2. For Presta, unscrew the top nut, then press the pin at the tip briefly to release air.
3. For Schrader, press the pin in the center with a fingernail or the tip of a key.

## Step 3: Get the tire off the rim

1. Push the tire bead (the edge that sits in the rim) toward the center of the rim on both sides. Start opposite the valve and work toward it.
2. Insert one tire lever under the bead next to the valve. Hook the lever onto a spoke to hold it.
3. Insert a second lever a few spokes away and pry the bead up over the rim edge.
4. Keep the second lever in place and work around the rim with it, if needed.
5. Do not use screwdrivers or metal tools near the tube. They cut tubes easily.

## Step 4: Remove the tube

1. Pull the valve stem out of the rim hole first.
2. Pull the rest of the tube out from inside the tire.
3. Leave the tire on one side of the rim if possible. It is easier to put back on.

## Step 5: Find the hole

1. Add a small amount of air to the tube, just enough to give it shape.
2. Listen for a hiss, or run the tube slowly across your cheek or through a puddle to feel or see bubbles.
3. When you find the leak, mark it with a pen or a small piece of tape.
4. Dry the tube before you patch it.

## Step 6: Find what caused the flat

1. Check the inside of the tire carefully with your fingers. Feel for thorns, glass, wire, or sharp stones.
2. Remove anything you find. If you leave it, it will puncture the new patch.
3. Check the rim tape (the strip inside the rim covering the spoke ends). If a spoke end pokes through, cover it with tape or move the tube.
4. If the tire has a cut, put a tire boot inside the tire over the cut. Fold a dollar bill or a piece of cloth to fit.

1. Sand the area around the hole, a little larger than the patch. Sand in small circles until the surface looks dull and rough.
2. Wipe the area clean with a dry rag or alcohol wipe. Do not touch it with your fingers.

4. Wait until the glue is tacky. It should feel sticky but not wet, usually about one to two minutes. Follow the instructions in your kit.
5. Peel the foil off the back of the patch without touching the adhesive side.
6. Press the patch firmly onto the glue, centered on the hole. Hold it for at least 30 seconds.
7. If the kit includes talc powder, dust a little over the patch edges to stop them sticking to the tire.

1. Add a small amount of air to the tube so it keeps its shape. Do not fill it fully yet.
2. Insert the valve into the rim hole first, then tuck the rest of the tube inside the tire.
3. Make sure the tube is not twisted and is not caught under the tire edge.
4. Push one side of the tire bead back onto the rim, starting opposite the valve and working toward it. Use your thumbs first.
5. Push the other side of the bead onto the rim the same way. Finish the last section with your thumbs. Use a tire lever only for the last few centimeters, and never pinch the tube.
6. Check that the bead sits evenly on both sides of the rim.

## Step 9: Inflate the tire

1. Pump the tire to the pressure printed on the sidewall. Pumping a little at a time keeps the bead seated.
2. Spin the wheel and watch the tire. It should not wobble or bulge. If it bulges, let out the air and check that the tube is not pinched.

4. Reconnect or close the brake.
5. Spin the wheel. It should turn freely and not rub the brake pads or frame.
6. Squeeze the brake to check it stops the wheel.

1. Ride slowly for a short distance and listen for rubbing.
2. Check the brakes and the gears.
3. Keep the patch kit and a pump with you for the rest of the ride.

# Bike Tour Packing Guide (7 days)

Assumptions: you ride your own bike, you fly with it in a box or case, you carry everything on the bike, and you sleep in a mix of camp sites and hotels. If your plan differs, the reasons below still apply, but some items will change.

## 1. Bike and flight prep

* **Bike box or hard case.** Airlines damage bikes that travel loose or in thin cardboard. A hard case or a sturdy box protects the frame and derailleur.
* **Remove pedals, turn the handlebars, drop the seat, and deflate tires to about half pressure.** These steps shrink the bike so it fits the box. Lower tire pressure protects the rims if the box gets knocked.
* **Wrap the chain and derailleur, and add a spare derailleur hanger.** A bent hanger ends a tour early, and a spare is cheap insurance.
* **Pedal wrench, hex keys, and a multitool.** You need these to reassemble the bike at the airport and to fix small problems on the road.
* **Check airline rules for tools and CO2 cartridges.** Rules vary by airline and country, and some items may need to go in checked bags. Confirm before you pack them.

## 2. Repair kit (carry this on the bike)

* **Two spare inner tubes, matching your tire size.** Flat tires are the most common roadside problem. Two tubes cover two flats without a shop visit.
* **Tire levers (two or three), patch kit, and a pump.** A pump lets you fix a flat without a cartridge. Patches fix a tube that gets punctured again.
* **Spare quick link or chain tool, and a spare set of brake pads.** A broken chain stops the bike completely. Worn pads can fail on long descents.
* **Spoke wrench and a few zip ties.** Zip ties hold a broken mount, a rack, or a cable in place.
* **Duct tape, wrapped around a pump or a water bottle.** It covers a damaged tire wall or a torn bag.

## 3. Clothing

* **Two or three padded cycling kits (shorts and jersey).** Padding reduces saddle soreness, which is the main comfort problem on multi-day rides. Rotating kits lets you wash one each night.
* **Four to five pairs of cycling socks.** Dry socks prevent blisters, which can stop a rider on day three.
* **Rain jacket, and a warm layer such as a fleece or light down jacket.** Mornings and mountain passes are often colder than the afternoon, and rain can come with little warning.
* **Arm warmers or a light long-sleeve top.** These cover the cold early hours and pack small.
* **Full-finger gloves, a cap or sun hat, and sunglasses.** Gloves protect your hands in a fall. Sunglasses block grit and glare.
* **One set of casual clothes for evenings.** You need something clean to wear off the bike.
* **Sleep clothes and a small towel.** They keep you comfortable in camp or hotel rooms.

## 4. Sleep (if you camp)

* **Tent or bivvy, sleeping bag rated for the coldest night, and a sleeping pad.** The pad insulates you from the ground, which matters more than the bag on cold nights. Rate the bag for the lowest temperature you expect.
* **Compression sacks.** They shrink bulky gear so it fits in bags on the bike.

## 5. Health and toiletries

* **Sunscreen, lip balm, and chamois cream.** Sun burns on long rides are common. Chamois cream reduces chafing under the shorts.
* **Personal medications, plus a small first aid kit.** Include bandages, antiseptic, blister plasters, and pain relief. Pack a few days of medication beyond the trip length in case of delays.
* **Electrolyte tablets and a small bottle of antiseptic wipes.** Heat and long days drain salts. Wipes clean road rash and sweat without water.
* **Toothbrush, deodorant, and a small bottle of soap.** These cover basic hygiene in camp or hotels.

## 6. Electronics

* **Phone, charger, cable, and a power bank.** Phones drain quickly with navigation running. Carry enough power for a full day of use.
* **Front and rear bike lights, and a headlamp.** Lights are required for riding in low light and in tunnels. A headlamp helps at camp and fixes problems after dark.
* **Offline maps and route files, downloaded before you fly.** Mobile signal fails in rural areas, and offline files still work.
* **Plug adapter.** Outlets differ by country.

## 7. Documents and money

* **Passport or ID, flight and hotel bookings, and a travel insurance policy.** Insurance covers bike damage, medical costs, and trip cancellation. Check whether it covers cycling.
* **Bank cards, some local cash, and a photo or printed copy of your documents.** Copies help if the originals are lost.
* **Emergency contact list on paper.** It works when the phone does not.

## 8. Water and food

* **Two water bottles and two cages.** Two bottles carry enough water for long, hot stages. Cages keep them secure on rough roads.
* **Snacks for the bike, such as bars, nuts, or dried fruit.** Riders run low on energy between towns, and planned snacks prevent bonks.

## 9. Packing method

* **Heavy items low and close to the center of the bike.** Weight low and central keeps the handling stable, especially on descents.
* **Waterproof bags or dry bags for clothes and sleep gear.** Rain soaks ordinary bags quickly.
* **Keep the repair kit, lights, documents, and medications in your carry-on.** These items are hard or impossible to replace quickly, and a checked bag can be delayed.
* **Balance the load between two sides.** Uneven panniers pull the bike to one side and wear the wheel on that side.

## 10. Final check before you board

* Bike box sealed and labeled with your name and destination.
* Tools, spare tubes, and repair kit packed in the right bags.
* Documents, insurance, and offline maps saved on your phone and on paper.
* Medications and chargers in your carry-on.

* **One set of casual clothes for evenings.** You need something clean to wear off the bike.
* **Sleep clothes and a small towel.** They keep you comfortable in camp or hotel rooms.

* **Plug adapter.** Outlets differ by country.

* **Passport or ID, flight and hotel bookings, and a travel insurance policy.** Insurance covers bike damage, medical costs, and trip cancellation. Check whether it covers cycling.

* **Emergency contact list on paper.** It works when the phone does not.

## 8. Water and food

* **Two water bottles and two cages.** Two bottles carry enough water for long, hot stages. Cages keep them secure on rough roads.

* **Heavy items low and close to the center of the bike.** Weight low and central keeps the handling stable, especially on descents.

* **Balance the load between two sides.** Uneven panniers pull the bike to one side and wear the wheel on that side.

* Bike box sealed and labeled with your name and destination.
* Tools, spare tubes, and repair kit packed in the right bags.
* Documents, insurance, and offline maps saved on your phone and on paper.
* Medications and chargers in your carry-on.

# Chain and Cassette Wear: Class Guide

## Why chains wear out

A bike chain is a row of small steel pins, rollers, and side plates. Each link pivots thousands of times per ride. Grit from the road gets between the pins and rollers and grinds them down. Each pin wears a tiny amount, and the chain stretches. The chain does not actually get longer. The pins wear, so the gap between them grows. Over time, the chain no longer fits the teeth of the cassette and chainring properly.

Dirt, sand, and water speed this up. Dry or dirty lube does the same. Regular cleaning and lubrication slow wear a lot.

## How to measure wear

Use a chain wear indicator tool (a "chain checker"). It has a hook that sits in the chain rollers.

1. Clean the chain so the tool seats properly.
2. Place the hook in a roller and let it drop in.
3. Check the scale or the indicator reading.

At 0.5 percent wear, the chain is still in good shape. At 0.75 percent, it is worn and should be replaced soon. Many shops replace at 0.75 percent to protect the cassette.

If you have no checker, measure 12 inches (or 24 links) in the chain. A new chain measures exactly 12.0 inches between the pin centers. A chain that measures 12.1 inches or more is worn. Note that a ruler is less accurate than a checker.

## When to replace the chain

- The checker reads 0.75 percent or more.
- The chain skips under pedaling load, especially on the largest cogs.
- The chain sticks, stiffens, or has stiff links that do not move freely after cleaning.
- The chain has a rusty or damaged link.

Replace the chain before the cassette is worn. A new chain on a worn cassette will skip.

## Why the cassette wears

Worn chain pins do not seat deeply between the cassette teeth. The chain then rides up the tooth and pushes the teeth to wear into a hooked shape. This wear happens slowly, and it can happen to the chainring too.

## When to replace the cassette

- Teeth look hooked, pointed, or shark-fin shaped.
- A new chain skips on the cassette, especially under load.
- The cassette has visible wear on the teeth or missing teeth.
- Replace the cassette when you replace the second or third chain. Many cassettes last through two or three chains.

For cassette wear, always inspect the cassette before replacing the chain.

## Quick checklist

1. Measure the chain every 300 to 500 miles (500 to 800 km).
2. Replace the chain at 0.75 percent wear.
3. Inspect the cassette when replacing the chain.
4. Replace the cassette if the teeth are hooked or a new chain skips.

# Chain and Cassette Wear: Class Guide

## Why chains wear out

A bike chain is a row of small steel pins, rollers, and side plates. Each link pivots thousands of times per ride. Grit from the road gets between the pins and rollers and grinds them down. Each pin wears a tiny amount, and the chain stretches. The chain does not actually get longer. The pins wear, so the gap between them grows. Over time, the chain no longer fits the teeth of the cassette and chainring properly.

Dirt, sand, and water speed this up. Dry or dirty lube does the same. Regular cleaning and lubrication slow wear a lot.

## How to measure wear

Use a chain wear indicator tool (a "chain checker"). It has a hook that sits in the chain rollers.

1. Clean the chain so the tool seats properly.
2. Place the hook in a roller and let it drop in.
3. Check the scale or the indicator reading.

At 0.5 percent wear, the chain is still in good shape. At 0.75 percent, it is worn and should be replaced soon. Many shops replace at 0.75 percent to protect the cassette.

If you have no checker, measure 12 inches (or 24 links) in the chain. A new chain measures exactly 12.0 inches between the pin centers. A chain that measures 12.1 inches or more is worn. Note that a ruler is less accurate than a checker.

## When to replace the chain

- The checker reads 0.75 percent or more.
- The chain skips under pedaling load, especially on the largest cogs.
- The chain sticks, stiffens, or has stiff links that do not move freely after cleaning.
- The chain has a rusty or damaged link.

Replace the chain before the cassette is worn. A new chain on a worn cassette will skip.

## Why the cassette wears

Worn chain pins do not seat deeply between the cassette teeth. The chain then rides up the tooth and pushes the teeth to wear into a hooked shape. This wear happens slowly, and it can happen to the chainring too.

## When to replace the cassette

- Teeth look hooked, pointed, or shark-fin shaped.
- A new chain skips on the cassette, especially under load.
- The cassette has visible wear on the teeth or missing teeth.
- Replace the cassette when you replace the second or third chain. Many cassettes last through two or three chains.

For cassette wear, always inspect the cassette before replacing the chain.

## Quick checklist

1. Measure the chain every 300 to 500 miles (500 to 800 km).
2. Replace the chain at 0.75 percent wear.
3. Inspect the cassette when replacing the chain.
4. Replace the cassette if the teeth are hooked or a new chain skips.

# Winter Storage Routine

## Cleaning

Before storing your bike, wash off road grime, salt, and mud with a bucket of warm water and mild soap. Rinse with a hose on low pressure and keep water away from the bearings and the headset. Dry the frame, chain, and cassette fully with a clean cloth. Wipe the brake pads and rims so no grit stays on the braking surfaces. Clean the drivetrain with a degreaser and a brush, then rinse and dry it, since winter grime wears chains quickly if it is left in place.

## Lubrication

Once the drivetrain is dry, apply a light coat of chain lube to each link, then wipe off the excess with a rag so the chain does not collect dust. Put a few drops of oil on the derailleur pivots and the brake and shifter cable housings. Lightly grease the seatpost and the pedal threads so they do not seize. Check the bottom bracket and headset for play, and do not over-grease them. A thin, even layer of lubricant is enough to protect the parts through the season.

## Tires

Check the tire pressure and drop it slightly, to about two thirds of the normal riding pressure, so the tires are not under constant strain. Inspect the tread and sidewalls for cracks, cuts, and embedded glass, and replace any damaged tire before spring. If the bike will sit for several months, hang it from the frame or lift it onto a stand so that no tire rests on the ground. This prevents flat spots and keeps the rubber from hardening.

## Where to Keep the Bike

Store the bike indoors in a dry place with a stable temperature, such as a closet, basement room, or garage that does not freeze. Avoid unheated sheds, balconies, and areas exposed to rain or snow, because moisture speeds up rust and corrosion. Keep the bike away from heaters and direct sunlight, which can crack rubber and dry out grease. Hang the bike on a wall hook or a stand, and cover it loosely with a breathable cloth or sheet to keep dust off the components.

# Torque Wrench Guide for Bicycles

## What a torque wrench is for

A torque wrench measures how hard a fastener is tightened. Bolts on a bike clamp parts together through friction, and the clamping force comes from the bolt stretching a small amount. Torque is the proxy for that clamping force. Too little torque lets parts slip, rattle, or come loose. Too much torque can crush carbon fiber, strip threads, stretch or snap bolts, or warp a part under load.

Most bike parts list a torque value in Newton meters (Nm) on the part itself, on the box, or in the manufacturer's manual. That printed value overrides any table, including the one below. Carbon parts are the most sensitive, so always check their markings.

## Types of torque wrench

- Click type: the most common. It clicks when the set torque is reached. Set it back to the lowest setting after use so the spring stays calibrated.
- Beam type: a pointer on a scale. Cheap and reliable, but you need to read the scale while you pull.
- Digital: shows live torque and often beeps at the target. Good for carbon work.
- Bit or socket type: use the correct hex or Torx bit. A worn bit can slip and give a false reading.

Use a torque wrench with a range that covers the value you need. A 2 to 10 Nm wrench is the usual bike tool. Pedals and crank bolts need a higher range, typically 30 to 60 Nm.

## Why torque matters on a bike

- Carbon parts (bars, stems, seatposts, frames): overtightening cracks the fiber without visible damage. The part may fail later under load.
- Threads: aluminum and steel threads strip when overtightened. Stripped threads in a frame or crank often mean replacement.
- Slipping: undertightened stems, seatposts, and handlebars can rotate under load, which is a crash risk.
- Thread lubricants: anti-seize, grease, and carbon assembly paste change the friction of the threads. Use the lubricant the manufacturer specifies, because the same torque applied with a different lubricant gives a different clamp force.

## Common torque values across a bike

These are typical ranges from common manufacturers. Verify against the markings on the specific part.

### Cockpit

| Part | Typical value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Stem faceplate bolts (to bar) | 5 Nm (4 to 6 Nm) | Holds the bar in the stem. Carbon bars are the most sensitive. |
| Stem steerer clamp bolts | 5 Nm (4 to 6 Nm) | Clamps the stem to the fork steerer. Overtightening can crack carbon steerers. |
| Handlebar bar-end plug or bar end | 4 to 6 Nm | Keeps the bar end secure without crushing it. |
| Brake lever clamp to bar | 2 to 5 Nm (often 2 to 3 Nm on carbon bars) | Holds the lever in place. Too tight can crack carbon bars. |
| Shifter or STI clamp | 2 to 3 Nm | Light clamp, easy to crush. |
| Headset top cap or stem top bolt | Set preload, then torque the top bolt to the stem spec (about 5 Nm) | Preload sets the headset bearings. Check the headset maker's preload method. |

### Seat and saddle

| Part | Typical value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Seatpost clamp bolts | 5 to 6 Nm (carbon often 5 Nm) | Holds the post in the frame. Too little lets the post slip. |
| Saddle rail clamp | 4 to 6 Nm (often 5 Nm) | Holds the saddle rails. Overtightening can crack carbon rails. |

### Brakes

| Part | Typical value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Post mount caliper bolts | 6 to 8 Nm | Holds the caliper to the fork or frame. Under torque can cause brake shudder. |
| Rotor bolts (6 bolt) | 2.5 to 6 Nm depending on brand | Holds the rotor to the hub. Too tight can warp the rotor. |
| Center lock lockring | 40 Nm (about 35 to 50 Nm) | Holds the rotor to the hub with a lockring. Undertightened rotors can wobble or come loose. |

### Wheels and drivetrain

| Part | Typical value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Thru axle | 10 to 15 Nm | Holds the wheel in the fork or frame. Too loose can let the wheel move. |
| Quick release | Set by lever force, not torque | Follow the lever tension marks. Not a torque bolt. |
| Cassette lockring | 30 to 50 Nm (often 40 Nm) | Holds the cassette on the freehub. Too loose lets cogs shift. |
| Chainring bolts | 8 to 12 Nm | Holds chainrings to the crank spider. Too tight can crack the spider. |
| Crank arm bolt (square taper or Hollowtech) | 35 to 50 Nm | Holds the crank on the spindle. Under torque can let the crank loosen. |
| Pedals | 35 Nm (30 to 35 Nm) | Holds the pedal in the crank. Use the 15 mm wrench flat and grease the threads if the maker says so. |
| Front derailleur clamp or mount bolt | 5 to 7 Nm | Holds the derailleur to the frame. Too tight can deform the clamp. |
| Rear derailleur mount bolt | 8 to 10 Nm | Holds the derailleur hanger to the frame. Too loose lets the derailleur shift out of position. |

### Frame and bottom bracket

| Part | Typical value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Threaded bottom bracket cups | 35 to 50 Nm | Holds the bottom bracket in the frame shell. Use the manufacturer's value and thread lubricant. |
| Press fit bottom bracket | Not torqued | Pressed in and held by interference fit. Use the press tool. |
| Water bottle cage bolts | 1 to 2 Nm | Light fastener. Overtightening can crack carbon frames or strip threads. |
| Rack or fender bolts | 5 to 8 Nm | Holds racks and fenders. Mounting points on aluminum are often rated at a lower value. |

## Practical notes

- Tighten in small steps and in a cross pattern when a part has multiple bolts, such as a faceplate stem or rotor.
- Clean and dry the threads unless the manual calls for grease or paste.
- Torque the bolts after the part is positioned. Do not tighten one bolt fully and then align the part.
- Check torque on carbon parts after the first few rides, and after any crash or change in position.
- If the value is not printed on the part, use the manufacturer's manual or website. If neither is available, use a mid range value and do not exceed the lower limit of the range for carbon parts.

# Torque Wrench Guide for Bicycles

## What a torque wrench is for

A torque wrench measures how hard a fastener is tightened. Bolts on a bike clamp parts together through friction, and the clamping force comes from the bolt stretching a small amount. Torque is the proxy for that clamping force. Too little torque lets parts slip, rattle, or come loose. Too much torque can crush carbon fiber, strip threads, stretch or snap bolts, or warp a part under load.

Most bike parts list a torque value in Newton meters (Nm) on the part itself, on the box, or in the manufacturer's manual. That printed value overrides any table, including the one below. Carbon parts are the most sensitive, so always check their markings.

## Types of torque wrench

- Click type: the most common. It clicks when the set torque is reached. Set it back to the lowest setting after use so the spring stays calibrated.
- Beam type: a pointer on a scale. Cheap and reliable, but you need to read the scale while you pull.
- Digital: shows live torque and often beeps at the target. Good for carbon work.
- Bit or socket type: use the correct hex or Torx bit. A worn bit can slip and give a false reading.

Use a torque wrench with a range that covers the value you need. A 2 to 10 Nm wrench is the usual bike tool. Pedals and crank bolts need a higher range, typically 30 to 60 Nm.

## Why torque matters on a bike

- Carbon parts (bars, stems, seatposts, frames): overtightening cracks the fiber without visible damage. The part may fail later under load.
- Threads: aluminum and steel threads strip when overtightened. Stripped threads in a frame or crank often mean replacement.
- Slipping: undertightened stems, seatposts, and handlebars can rotate under load, which is a crash risk.
- Thread lubricants: anti-seize, grease, and carbon assembly paste change the friction of the threads. Use the lubricant the manufacturer specifies, because the same torque applied with a different lubricant gives a different clamp force.

# Online Parts Order Form

The online parts order form lets members and walk-in customers of Fern Hollow Bicycle Cooperative request parts from our shelves before they visit the shop. A customer picks a part by its SKU, enters a quantity, and chooses a pickup day. The form checks each request against the current inventory count, so people only see parts we have in stock. Once a request is submitted, a volunteer at the counter receives it, pulls the parts from the bay listed for each SKU, and sets the order aside under the customer's name. The form also shows a short status line for each order, such as received, ready for pickup, or held for repair, so customers know where their order stands without calling the shop.

# Fern Hollow Bicycle Cooperative: Brake Check Procedure for New Volunteers

Read this whole page before you touch a bike. If anything looks unsafe and you are not sure, stop, tag the bike as held, and get a lead mechanic.

## Before you start

1. Wear eye protection. Brake pads and rotors can throw debris.
2. Spin the wheel and look at the brake pads and rim or rotor first, so you know what you are checking.
3. Confirm the bike is not held for repair. Check the tag or the work log.
4. Note which brake type the bike has. Rim brakes clamp the wheel rim. Disc brakes clamp a rotor bolted to the hub.

## Part A: Rim brakes

### A1. Pad condition
- Look at each brake pad from the side. Pad rubber should be at least 1 mm thick above the wear line or groove.
- Replace the pad if the rubber is hard, cracked, glazed, or has grit stuck in it.
- Pads must be free of oil and grease. Oil on a pad means the pad must be replaced and the rim cleaned.

### A2. Pad alignment
- The pad should contact the rim braking surface only. It should not touch the tire sidewall or the tire.
- The leading edge of the pad (the front edge the rim meets first when it rolls forward) should sit about 1 mm lower than the trailing edge. This is called toe in. It stops squeal and makes the pad grip evenly.
- Tighten the pad bolt so the pad does not rotate when you squeeze the lever hard.

### A3. Rim condition
- Spin the wheel and look at the braking surface. It should be smooth and the same width all the way around.
- Look for cracks, bulges, or a dark ring on the braking surface. A wear indicator groove that is worn through means the rim is near the end of its life. Hold the bike and get a lead mechanic.
- Check that the rim is clean. Wipe it with a clean rag and rubbing alcohol if it has grease.

### A4. Centering and clearance
- Squeeze the lever. Both pads should close at the same time and reach the rim at the same distance.
- Release the lever. Both pads should return with clearance of about 1 to 2 mm from the rim. The wheel should spin without rubbing.
- Adjust the centering screw on the caliper until the pads sit evenly on both sides.

### A5. Cable and lever
- Pull the lever. It should stop at least 2 cm before it touches the handlebar.
- The cable should move freely through the housing. Stiff or fraying cable means replace the cable or housing.
- Check the cable pinch bolt. It should be tight and the cable should not slip when you pull the lever.
- Check the cable housing ends for cracks and make sure the ferrules (small metal caps) are seated.

### A6. Brake test
- Lift the front wheel off the ground and spin it. Squeeze the front lever. The wheel should stop within one or two turns.
- Repeat for the rear wheel.
- Squeeze both levers at once. The bike should stop smoothly.

## Part B: Disc brakes

### B1. Pad condition
- Look through the caliper at the pads. Each pad should have at least 1 mm of friction material left. Many pads have a wear indicator groove or a metal wear tab. Replace the pads once they reach the indicator.
- Check that the pads are not contaminated with oil, grease, or brake fluid. Contaminated pads must be replaced. Do not try to clean them.
- Check that the pads are not glazed, cracked, or chunked.

### B2. Rotor condition
- Look at the rotor face. It should be flat and free of cracks, deep grooves, and blue or dark heat marks.
- Spin the wheel. Look for wobble or a rotor that touches the pads. A bent rotor needs to be trued or replaced.
- Check that all rotor bolts are present and tight. Use the torque value printed on the rotor or the manufacturer spec.
- Clean the rotor with isopropyl alcohol and a clean rag. Do not touch the braking surface with bare fingers.

### B3. Caliper alignment and mounting
- The caliper should be centered over the rotor. There should be an even gap on both sides of the rotor.
- Check the caliper mount bolts are tight. Use the manufacturer torque spec.
- Squeeze the lever and spin the wheel. It should not rub. If it rubs, loosen the caliper mount bolts, squeeze the lever to center the caliper, hold the lever, and retighten the bolts.

### B4. Hydraulic line and lever feel
- Look at the brake hose for cracks, bulges, or leaks at the fittings.
- Squeeze the lever. It should feel firm, and the lever should not pull to the bar. A spongy or soft lever usually means air in the system. Do not ride the bike. Get a lead mechanic to bleed the brake.
- Check the fluid level in the reservoir if the bike has one. Fluid should be between the minimum and maximum marks.

### B5. Mechanical disc brakes
- Pull the cable and check the cable pinch bolt. The cable should not slip.
- Check that the cable housing is not cracked and moves freely.

### B6. Brake test
- Lift the front wheel off the ground and spin it. Squeeze the front lever. The wheel should stop quickly and smoothly.
- Repeat for the rear wheel.
- Squeeze both levers at once. The bike should stop smoothly without pulling or grinding.
- Listen for grinding or squeal. Grinding often means pads are worn to metal. Stop and tag the bike.

## When to hold a bike

Tag the bike as held and tell a lead mechanic if you see any of these:
- Brake pads worn past the limit or contaminated
- Cracked rim or rotor, or a rim worn through its wear groove
- Cracked brake hose, cable, or housing
- Spongy or soft hydraulic lever
- Brake that does not stop the wheel in one or two turns
- Any bolt you cannot tighten to spec

## Sign off

Write the bike ID, brake type, what you checked, and your initials on the work log. Only sign off after your brake test passes.

# Chain and Cassette Wear

Class talk notes. Read top to bottom, about five minutes.

## Why chains wear out

A bicycle chain is a row of outer plates, inner plates, pins, and rollers. Each link pivots on a pin, and the roller sits around the pin so it can engage the teeth on the chainring and cassette.

Under load, the pins and the inside of the rollers rub against each other on every pedal stroke. Grit from road dirt and sand gets into those joints and works like sandpaper. When the lubricant is dried out or washed off, metal rubs on metal and wear speeds up.

As the pins wear, the distance between them grows. A chain does not stretch in the way a rubber band does. Its metal parts wear, so each pitch (the distance from one pin to the next) gets longer. The chain is still the same length in total, but the pitch no longer matches the cassette teeth, which the chain then rides over unevenly.

## How to measure wear

Use a chain wear indicator, such as a Park Tool CC-3.2 or a similar gauge. You can also measure by hand.

1. Clean the chain of grit and grease so the measurement is accurate.
2. Pull the chain gently forward on the chainring to remove slack.
3. Measure 24 pitches. On a standard 1/2 inch (12.7 mm) chain, 24 pitches equal exactly 12 inches (304.8 mm).
4. Check the measured length against 12.000 inches.
5. Calculate the percentage: (measured length minus 12.000) divided by 12.000, times 100.

Example: if the measurement is 12.09 inches, the wear is (12.09 minus 12.000) divided by 12.000, times 100, which is about 0.75 percent.

Measure in at least three spots on the chain and in different places around the loop, because wear is not always even.

## When to replace the chain

- Below 0.5 percent: the chain is in good shape. Check again in a few hundred miles or kilometers.
- 0.5 to 0.75 percent: the chain is wearing. Plan to replace it soon, especially before a long ride or a new cassette.
- 0.75 percent and above: replace the chain now. Riding a worn chain on a good cassette wears the cassette faster.
- Shifting that skips or jumps under load, or a chain that binds on a link, is a sign to replace the chain no matter what the gauge reads.

Replace the chain before it reaches 1 percent. Past that point, the chain can damage the cassette and chainrings.

## When to replace the cassette

The cassette wears to match a stretched chain. Look at the teeth, not the chain alone.

- Teeth that look hooked or pointed, shaped like a shark fin, are worn out.
- The chain skips or slips under pedaling load, especially on the largest cogs.
- The cassette is past about 1 percent chain wear, or a new chain skips on it.
- Teeth are visibly thin or hooked on more than one cog.

If the chain is worn but the cassette is not, replace only the chain. A new chain on a worn cassette will skip. If the cassette is worn, replace the chain at the same time, because a worn chain will ruin a new cassette quickly.

## Quick summary for class

- Chains wear at the pins and rollers, and each pitch gets longer.
- Measure 24 pitches. 12.000 inches is new. Read the percent of stretch.
- Replace the chain at 0.75 percent. Check the cassette before or when you replace the chain.
- Skipping under load means replace the chain and check the cassette, even if the gauge reads low.
